senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of strong opposition and displeasure against someone or something judged to be wrong
pertaining to not ceasing from some continuous activity
a painful feeling due to the consciousness of having done or experienced something disgraceful
senses.comment: In some languages ‘shame’ may be referred to by a descriptive expression, for example, ‘the feeling of being caught doing something bad’ or ‘the feeling of being seen while sinning.’ In other languages ‘shame’ is expressed idiomatically as ‘to hang the head’ or ‘to turn away the eyes’ or ‘to hide from people’s stares.’

senses.def: that which is or should be the source of shame or disgrace

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to act in defiance of social and moral standards, with resulting disgrace, embarrassment, and shame
senses.comment: Behavior involving disgrace, embarrassment, and shame is often expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bury one’s face,’ ‘to hide one’s eyes,’ or ‘to feel stabbed by people’s eyes.’ Since shame is seemingly a universal type of feeling, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory equivalent.

senses.def: (derivative of Ἀλεξανδρία ‘Alexandria,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Alexandria
a person for whom there is no record of a female parent or who has never had a female parent or whose mother has died
to cause something to become new and different, with the implication of becoming superior
the brother of Simon Peter and one of the twelve apostles
to join with and to maintain loyalty to
senses.comment: The degree of close association suggested by ἀντέχομαι in Matthew 6:24 is sometimes expressed idiomatically as ‘to stick oneself to,’ ‘to glue oneself to,’ or ‘to become one with.’

senses.def: to hold fast to a particular belief, with the implication of acting accordingly
to assist in supplying what may be needed
the totality of any object, mass, collective, or extension

to reestablish proper friendly interpersonal relations after these have been disrupted or broken (the componential features of this series of meanings involve (1) disruption of friendly relations because of (2) presumed or real provocation (3) overt behavior designed to remove hostility, and (4) restoration of original friendly relations)
glosses: to make things right with one another
senses.comment: Because of the variety and complexity of the components involved in reconciliation, it is often necessary to use an entire phrase in order to communicate satisfactorily the meanings of the terms in this subdomain. In some languages, however, reconciliation is often spoken of in idiomatic terms, for example, ‘to cause to become friends again,’ ‘to cause to snap fingers again’ (a symbol of friendly interpersonal relations in many parts of Africa), ‘to cause to be one again,’ or ‘to take away the separation.’ A particularly crucial element in terms for reconciliation is the assigning of responsibility for original guilt in causing the estrangement. Some terms, for example, imply that the individual who initiates reconciliation is by doing so admitting his guilt in causing the estrangement. This, of course, provides a completely untenable meaning for reconciliation in speaking of God reconciling people to himself through Christ.|In a number of languages the contextual basis for an expression for reconciliation is often found in terms relating to the reconciliation of husbands and wives. Such expressions fit in well with many contexts in the Scriptures, especially in speaking of reconciliation of people to God, since God is frequently referred to as the husband and the believers as the wife.

senses.def: to cause a load to be carried off

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a male partner in homosexual intercourse
senses.comment: It is possible that ἀρσενοκοίτης in certain contexts refers to the active male partner in homosexual intercourse in contrast with μαλακός[b], the passive male partner (88.281).

senses.def: to go astray as the result of departing from the truth
to remove the guilt resulting from wrongdoing
senses.comment: It is extremely important to note that the focus in the meanings of ἀφίημι[f], ἄφεσις[a], and ἀπολύω[e] is upon the guilt of the wrongdoer and not upon the wrongdoing itself. The event of wrongdoing is not undone, but the guilt resulting from such an event is pardoned. To forgive, therefore, means essentially to remove the guilt resulting from wrongdoing.|Some languages make a clear distinction between guilt and sin, and terms for forgiveness are therefore related to guilt and not to the wrongdoing. Therefore, ‘to forgive sins’ is literally ‘to forgive guilt.’ Though terms for ‘forgiveness’ are often literally ‘to wipe out,’ ‘to blot out,’ or ‘to do away with,’ it is obviously not possible to blot out or to wipe out an event, but it is possible to remove or obliterate the guilt.

senses.def: the process of setting free or liberating
an additional name of a certain Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus who was an associate of Paul
to consume solid food
an altar with a base or pedestal; for offering sacrifices to a god
senses.comment: In this only reference in the NT in which βωμός occurs, the altar to the Unknown God may be spoken of as ‘a place for offerings to a god whom people do not know’ or ‘… god whose name is not known.’

senses.def: pertaining to being sweet in contrast with being bitter or salty
senses.comment: In a number of languages it would be somewhat misleading to speak of ‘sweet water,’ since this would suggest water to which sugar or some other sweet substance had been added. The equivalent in James 3:11 may be ‘fresh water’ or ‘good water’ in contrast with ‘bad water’ or ‘not bitter water’ in contrast with ‘bitter water.’

senses.def: a marker of an additive relation, but with the possible implication of some contrast
marker of a sequence of closely related events
a marker of contrast
a marker of two or more items which are additively related and thematically parallel
a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another
glosses: on the one hand … but on the other hand

senses.def: to bring a formal or informal complaint, normally to a third person, with the implication that the individual against whom the complaint is made has been guilty of doing something wrong
to cause a group or gathering to disperse or scatter, with possible emphasis on the distributive nature of the scattering (that is to say, each going in a different direction)
a relatively emphatic marker of result, usually denoting the fact that the inference is self-evident
(derivative of δύναμαι ‘to be able,’ 74.5) to cause someone to have the ability to do or to experience something
the offspring of one’s children
senses.comment: In the one passage in which ἔκγονος occurs in the NT (namely, 1 Timothy 5:4), the reference is to adult grandchildren, and in some languages this element in the meaning must be made explicit. In languages in which there is no generic term to include both ‘grandsons’ and ‘granddaughters,’ it may be necessary to translate ἔκγονος in 1 Timothy 5:4 as ‘grandsons or granddaughters.’

senses.def: to remove a plant, including its roots
glosses: to pull out by the roots

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: pertaining to what is Greek
senses.comment: In rendering this expression in Revelation 9:11 it is often necessary to say ‘in the language spoken by the Greeks’ or ‘in the Greek language.’ Ελληνικός as an adjective does not denote the Greek language as such, but in the feminine form the reference would be to γλῶσσα ‘language.’

senses.def: to put on clothes, without implying any particular article of clothing
to listen carefully to and pay attention
to exert intense effort on behalf of something
to add to, with the implication of some reorganization or rearrangement
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘adding something to a covenant’ would be rendered as ‘to say that one must also do something else to fulfill the covenant.’

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a person of high status, particularly in view of a role of leadership
kid, he-goat in the singular and goats in the plural (in the plural form both male and female goats are included in the reference)
senses.comment: Since goats are so widely distributed throughout the world, there is usually little or no difficulty involved in finding a satisfactory term. The difficulty arises, however, in the connotations of the term for goat, especially in contrast with sheep. In contrast with usage in the Bible, in many parts of the tropical world goats are much more highly prized than sheep, because they can forage well for themselves and are appreciated for their meat. Sheep, on the other hand, are often regarded as scavengers and are much less valued. One should not reverse biblical statements about sheep and goats, but marginal notes and a fuller explanation of cultural differences in a glossary are important.

senses.def: to show reverent regard for
senses.comment: In εὐλαβέομαι[a] and εὐλάβεια there is also a certain element of awe, which may be interpreted in some instances as implying even fear. The implication of such reverent fear or awe is, of course, obedience, and some scholars prefer to interpret these terms in Hebrews 11:7 and Hebrews 5:7 as meaning ‘to obey’ (see 36.13) or ‘obedience.’

senses.def: (an Aramaic word)
senses.comment: The Aramaic word εφφαθα, together with the Greek interpretation ‘be opened,’ may still be relatively meaningless in the context of Mark 7:34 since it refers to the capacity for hearing.|In a number of languages one does not speak of a deaf person as ‘one whose ears are closed.’ The most appropriate equivalent may simply be ‘be able to hear’ or even ‘now you can hear.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: indefinite and multiple points of time, simultaneous with other corresponding points of time
to cause someone to recover health, often with the implication of having taken care of such a person
to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
senses.comment: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’

senses.def: one of the twelve apostles and the son of Zebedee and brother of John
a brother of Jesus
the son of Alphaeus and one of the twelve apostles
senses.comment: Some scholars consider Ἰάκωβος[c] and Ἰάκωβος[d] to be the same person.

senses.def: the son of Mary[d] and called ‘the younger’ in Mark 15:40
senses.comment: Some scholars consider Ἰάκωβος[c] and Ἰάκωβος[d] to be the same person.

senses.def: the father of Judas, one of the twelve apostles
a tax collector called ‘James’ rather than ‘Levi’ (Mark 2:14, apparatus)
Judas Iscariot, the betrayer of Jesus and one of the twelve apostles
Judas the son of James, and one of the twelve apostles
Judas, a brother of Jesus
Judas, Paul’s host in Damascus
Judas, called Barsabbas, a leading Christian in Jerusalem and a companion of Paul
Judas, a revolutionary leader
Judah, a person in the genealogy of Jesus
Judah, a son of Jacob in the genealogy of Jesus and an ancestor of an Israelite tribe
the tribe Judah
the territory of the tribe of Judah
act of cleansing from ritual contamination or impurity
senses.comment: The set of terms having the stem καθαρ appears to focus upon the elimination of ritual impurities. From an anthropological standpoint, this means the elimination of ritual contamination, or, in other words, negative taboo. This series of terms with the stem καθαρ appears to contrast with ἁγνίζω[a] and ἁγνισμός[a], ἁγιασμός[b], and ἅγιος[b] (53.44, 53.45, 53.46) focus upon a positive state of consecration and dedication to God and may be regarded as reflecting the acquisition of so-called positive taboo, that is to say, a state of holiness.

senses.def: an emphatic marker of concession
to speak against, often involving speaking evil of

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to become perverse or depraved, as a type of moral destruction
glosses: to cause the moral ruin of

senses.def: (derivative of κέραμος ‘potter’s clay,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to being made of potter’s clay
senses.comment: In some languages it may seem unduly repetitious to speak of ‘clay pots’ in Revelation 2:27 since a term for pot may refer only to objects made of clay. In biblical times, however, some σκεύη were of metal and others were of stone and wood. It may be possible to translate this expression in Revelation 2:27 as ‘they shall be broken like pots’ or ‘… like dishes.’

senses.def: any piece of furniture employed for reclining or lying on
senses.comment: In Matthew 9:2 a rendering such as ‘stretcher’ or ‘cot’ is certainly more advisable than the traditional rendering ‘bed,’ which might imply a large piece of furniture. In each passage one must employ a term which is most likely to identify the type of object which fits the context.

senses.def: one who rules over the whole world
senses.comment: The expression ‘world ruler’ should not be understood in terms of merely ruling over the earth as a physical object but of ‘ruling over those who are on the earth.’ Most scholars, however, interpret κοσμοκράτωρ in Ephesians 6:12 as meaning a supernatural power (see 12.44), though it is possible to understand κοσμοκράτωρ in this context as meaning a human ruler.

senses.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
senses.comment: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of Ephesians 1:21 some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

senses.def: probably the plant Cuminum cyminum; same family as carrot; branches from the base and has similar leaves and flowers, though seeds have a sharper smell; planted and harvested each year, reaching a height of about 50-60 cm; seeds are used in cooking and as medicine
senses.comment: In designating ‘cumin’ as well as ἄνηθον ‘dill,’ πήγανον ‘rue,’ and ἡδύοσμον ‘mint,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called cumin.’

senses.def: a dreaded condition of the skin, including what is now regarded as leprosy, as well as certain other types of infectious skin diseases, resulting in a person’s being regarded as ceremonially unclean and thus excluded from normal relations with other people
a tetrarch of Abilene

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: a smooth, rounded concretion formed within the shells of certain mollusks and valued as a gem because of its lustrous color (see 2.29)
senses.comment: In general there is little difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘pearl,’ since such objects are relatively well known throughout the world. However, in some languages there is no term for ‘pearl,’ and therefore one may use in the case of Revelation 21:21 ‘beautiful white stones,’ and in Matthew 7:6 it may be appropriate to translate ‘do not throw your valuable jewels to pigs.’

senses.def: a feeling of apprehension or distress in view of possible danger or misfortune
senses.comment: For μέριμνα as part of an idiom in 1 Peter 5:7, see 25.250.|The term μέριμνα may refer to either unnecessary worry or legitimate concern. The equivalent of ‘worry’ may be expressed in some languages in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to be killed by one’s mind’ or ‘to be pained by thinking.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to cast cares upon) to stop worrying and to put one’s trust in someone
senses.comment: For another explanation of this expression in 1 Peter 5:7, taking only ἐπιρίπτω ἐπί as an idiom, see 90.18.

senses.def: to increase in length, restricted in the NT to the growth of plants
the young of cattle
senses.comment: In Greek outside of the NT μόσχος is either masculine or feminine, but in the NT the forms are either masculine (Luke 15:23) or the distinction is not indicated by the accompanying grammatical forms (Hebrews 9:12).|In languages spoken by cattle-raising people, the major difficulty is in finding a satisfactory generic expression, since the tendency is to be very specific in matters of age, sex, color, size, etc. Under such circumstances one can only select terms with more or less generic meanings or employ more specific expressions which seem to fit particular contexts.

senses.def: a marker of the basis for an oath or strong declaration
senses.comment: Because of the elliptical nature of this expression in 1 Corinthians 15:31, the semantic implications of νή are often omitted, or the implication of νή is introduced by employing an overt declaration, as in Today’s English Version, “The pride I have in you, in our life in union with Christ Jesus our Lord, makes me declare this.”

senses.def: the state of having little or inadequate faith
an event in which something appears vividly and credibly to the mind, although not actually present, but implying the influence of some divine or supernatural power or agency
a marker of result, often implying the conclusion of a process of reasoning
a marker of somewhat greater emphasis (in comparison with μέν[b], γέ, and δή, 91.6)
a marker of relatively weak contrast
senses.comment: In a context such as John 9:18, ὅτι may also serve as a type of transition.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: trickery involving evil cunning

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: what a person has done in transgressing the will and law of God by some false step or failure
one’s biological or adoptive male parent
senses.comment: In some languages it may be necessary to distinguish clearly between a term for one’s biological father and an expression which refers to one’s legal father.

senses.def: biological or legal parents
senses.comment: In a number of instances it may be necessary to translate ‘parents’ as simply ‘father and mother.’

senses.def: a person several preceding generations removed from the reference person
senses.comment: In a number of languages one’s forefathers may be referred to simply as ‘fathers who have long since died.’ In other languages they may be referred to as ‘fathers of other generations’ or ‘fathers of ancient times.’

senses.def: (title for God, literally: father) one who combines aspects of supernatural authority and care for his people
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to distinguish clearly between ‘Father’ when referring to the heavenly Father and ‘father’ as a reference to a human father. The use of capitalization is quite satisfactory for the individual who is reading a text but not for one who is hearing it read, and since more people hear a text read than read it for themselves, it is essential that the reference of ‘Father’ be clear. In order to identify the use of ‘Father’ as a title for God, it is possible in many languages to use ‘Father in heaven’ or ‘Father above’ or ‘Father God.’|In some languages it may even be necessary to identify the ‘Father’ as the creator and therefore employ a phrase such as ‘our Father who created us.’|A particularly complicating factor involved in the use of ‘Father’ as a title for God is its occurrence without a pronominal reference as to whose father is involved. For example, in a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘father’ without indicating whose father, because a person does not become a father except by some relationship to another individual. Therefore, one must always speak of ‘my father’ or ‘his father’ and never simply ‘the father.’ In passages in which Jesus is speaking of ‘the Father’ in relationship to himself, it is necessary usually to employ a phrase such as ‘my Father.’ When, however, ‘Father’ is used as a title for ‘God’ in his relationship to people generally, then one may speak of ‘our Father’ (normally with an inclusive first person plural pronoun if the language in question makes a distinction between inclusive and exclusive first person plural pronoun referents).

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a title for a person of high rank

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a member of a well-defined socio-religious entity and representing an older age group than the so-called reference person
(figurative extension of meaning of πατήρ[a] ‘father,’ 10.14) an archetype anticipating a later reality and suggesting a derivative relationship
(a figurative extension of meaning of πατήρ[a] ‘father,’ 10.14) one who is responsible for having guided another into faith or into a particular pattern of behavior
(a Semitic idiom, literally: to place with his fathers) to carry out a burial procedure
to have a belt or sash around oneself
(an idiom, literally: to gird up the loins) to cause oneself to be in a state of readiness
senses.comment: In the context of Ephesians 6:14, it may be useful to preserve the extended figure of readiness for warfare beginning with Ephesians 6:13 and extending through Ephesians 6:17.

senses.def: to cause something to become bitter

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of πικρία[b] ‘bitterness,’ 88.201) to have bitter resentment or hatred toward someone else
(derivative of πνεῦμα[a] ‘Spirit,’ 12.18) pertaining to being derived from or being about the Spirit, in reference to such matters as gifts, benefits, teachings, blessings, and religious songs
senses.comment: The reference in 1 Corinthians 2:14 may be interpreted to mean that the unspiritual person cannot receive the gifts of the Spirit; neither can such a person understand them because they can only be judged or evaluated on the basis of their being derived from the Spirit of God. For another interpretation of πνευματικῶς in 1 Corinthians 2:14, see 26.10.

senses.def: pertaining to the spiritual nature or being of a person
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πνευματικῶς in 1 Corinthians 2:14, see 12.21.

senses.def: pertaining to expressions which are not to be understood literally, but symbolically or figuratively
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be more satisfactory to translate ἐν παραβολῇ and πνευματικῶς[c] by a negative expression, for example, ‘not literally’ or ‘not really.’ The expression in Revelation 11:8 might be translated as ‘that city might be called Sodom, but it isn’t really Sodom.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: an indefinite point of time or occasion
senses.comment: In John 9:13 ποτέ may be rendered as ‘had been,’ but the meaning is simply indefinite reference to time.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is roughly simultaneous to or overlaps with another point of time

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: some point of time selected in advance
to begin an association with someone, whether temporary or permanent
senses.comment: προσκληρόομαι in a context such as Acts 17:4 may be rendered as ‘to throw in one’s lot with’ or ‘to identify themselves with’ or ‘to become a part of the same group as.’

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: a position or place of particular importance, implying special status to the person occupying it
a city north of Jerusalem
(derivative of σάλπιγξ[a] trumpet, 6.89) to produce sound with a trumpet
senses.comment: It is possible, of course, in Matthew 6:2 to interpret σαλπίζω as a type of causative and thus to say ‘to cause someone to blow the trumpet’ or ‘to have the trumpet blown.’

senses.def: to produce the sound of a trumpet (without specification of an agent)
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be best to render σαλπίσει in 1 Corinthians 15:52 as ‘people will hear the sound of the trumpet’ or ‘the sound of the trumpet will be heard.’

senses.def: (derivative of σίδηρος ‘iron,’ 2.58) pertaining to being made or consisting of iron

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: (derivative of σμάραγδος emerald, 2.33) consisting of emerald, emerald-like, Revelation 4:3 (see 2.29)
pertaining to being solid or firm in contrast with that which is soft or liquid
pertaining to being firm and steadfast in one’s attitudes or beliefs
(a euphemistic figurative extension of meaning of συγκομίζω ‘to bring in a harvest,’ not occurring in the NT) to carry out arrangements for burial
to grow together with, in reference to plants
senses.comment: In rendering συναυξάνομαι (23.192) and συμφύομαι, it is important to avoid an expression which will imply that two plants grew together to become a single plant. The meaning is that two or more plants grew in the same general area and at approximately the same time.

senses.def: to indicate approval of a person or event, with the implication that others adopt the same attitude
to cause something to be known by action
senses.comment: In a number of languages the expression ‘to show oneself to be’ may best be rendered as ‘to cause people to know that one is,’ and therefore this expression in 2 Corinthians 6:4 may be rendered as ‘in everything causing people to know by what we do that we are servants of God.’

senses.def: to bring together or hold together something in its proper or appropriate place or relationship
senses.comment: In Colossians 1:17 it may not be easy to indicate clearly the relationship of the phrase ‘in him’ to the rest of the expression, namely, ‘all things hold together.’ Some translations have expanded the expression ‘in him’ to ‘in union with him’ or ‘in view of the fact that we are joined together with him.’|It is also possible to understand ἐν αὐτῷ as indicating agent, so that this expression in Colossians 1:17 may mean ‘by means of him all things hold together.’

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to stand together with someone
senses.comment: It is, of course, essential to avoid the idiomatic meaning of ‘to stand with’ in a sense of ‘to support.’ In this context the emphasis is simply upon being present with.

senses.def: to come into existence, with the implication of acquiring form and substance

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: (derivative of σῶμα[a] ‘body,’ 8.1) pertaining to a physical body
(figurative extension of meaning of τελευτάω ‘to end,’ not occurring in the NT) to come to the end of one’s life, as a euphemistic expression for death
an area of any size, regarded in certain contexts as a point in space
senses.comment: In John 11:48 the expression τὸν τόπον refers to the Temple in Jerusalem.

senses.def: a particular portion or unit of discourse
senses.comment: In rendering τόπος[b], περιοχή, or γραφή[a], it is often possible to use a rather general term such as the place or the part. In other instances one may wish to use a term meaning the words. Accordingly, Luke 4:21 may be rendered as ‘these words have come true today as you have heard them being read.’

senses.def: a role involving activity and responsibility
senses.comment: In some languages the latter part of this expression in Acts 1:25 may be rendered as ‘helping in this way and being an apostle’ or ‘helping in this way as an apostle.’ For another interpretation of τόπος in Acts 1:25, see 87.1.

senses.def: the position of a person within a group, implying a particular role or type of activity
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of this expression in Acts 1:25 may be simply ‘to undertake the work of an apostle’ or ‘to be an apostle in serving.’ For another interpretation of τόπος in Acts 1:25, involving a shift in focus, see 42.21.

senses.def: the possibility of some occasion or opportunity

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the inhabitants of a place
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to use a term meaning ‘place’ as a reference to the people of such a place.

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea
senses.def: a bar or reef produced in an area where two currents meet
senses.comment: It is possible to understand τόπος διθάλασσος in Acts 27:41 as a place of crosscurrents; see 14.32. In some languages it may be necessary to construct a descriptive equivalent for ‘sandbank,’ for example, ‘a hill of sand just beneath the surface of the water’ or ‘a ridge of sand hidden by the water.’

senses.def: (derivative of τυφῶν ‘Typhon,’ the legendary father of the winds, not occurring in the NT) pertaining to a very strong wind
senses.comment: Expressions for strong winds often differ on the basis of two important features: (1) the strength or violence of the wind and (2) the duration of the wind. For example, in English terms such as squall and tornado indicate violent but short periods of blowing, while hurricane or typhoon indicates a storm which takes a much longer period of time to pass. In Acts 27:14 the reference is obviously to the latter type of storm, called typhoon, hurricane, or monsoon, depending upon the region in which such violent and protracted storms occur.

senses.def: (derivative of ὑπακούω[a] ‘to obey,’ 36.15) pertaining to being obedient
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to showing hospitality to strangers
the nature of something as the result of its natural development or condition
senses.comment: For languages in which there is no ready equivalent to the lexical term ‘nature,’ it may be possible to render the expression in Galatians 4:8 as ‘beings who are really not gods,’ and in 2 Peter 1:4 one may translate ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to be like God in certain ways.’

senses.def: a class of entities based on physiological and genetic similarity
a person whose family members reported to Paul about divisions in the church in Corinth
one who claims to be the Christ or the Messiah but is not
